head: The kitchen moved
to the table.
slides.sub: How Benihana turned dinner into a show that paid for itself.

image.label: Flames rising from a teppanyaki grill in a dark room
image.brief: 어두운 식당 안, 철판 그릴 위로 불꽃이 솟는 순간. 셰프는 뒷모습 실루엣, 둘러앉은 손님들의 얼굴은 흐릿하게. 따뜻한 주황빛 영화 톤. 로고 없음.

head: A wrestler from Tokyo
in New York.
body: Rocky Aoki came to the United States from Japan as a young athlete. He reportedly saved money by running an ice cream truck in Manhattan.
In 1964 he opened a small restaurant on West 56th Street and named it Benihana, after his family’s café in Tokyo.

image.label: A 1960s Manhattan street with a small restaurant front
image.brief: 1960년대 맨해튼 거리의 작은 식당 입구. 노란 택시, 빈티지 간판(실제 로고 아님). 저녁 무렵 따뜻한 조명.

slides.label: tables in the first Benihana
body: It was tiny. And restaurants are hard: big kitchens, many cooks, wasted food, and tables that sit empty while diners linger. Most Americans then also knew little about Japanese food.

image.label: A small dining room with only a few tables
image.brief: 테이블 몇 개뿐인 작은 식당 내부. 1960년대 분위기, 비어 있는 의자들.

head: A small room, wary diners.
What do you serve?
body: You want Americans to try a Japanese restaurant, and you have very little space or money.

options.text: Serve familiar food like steak and shrimp, cooked by a chef at the table
options.feedback: Familiar food lowers the risk for diners, but it means giving up much of the traditional menu. Keep swiping.

options.text: Serve an authentic Japanese menu and educate diners
options.feedback: This is true to the cuisine, but it asks unsure customers to take a leap. Keep swiping.

options.text: Copy a classic American steakhouse with a Japanese name
options.feedback: Easy for diners to understand, but you’d be one more steakhouse in a crowded city. Keep swiping.

image.label: A chef’s knife and a raw steak on a cutting board
image.brief: 도마 위 칼과 생 스테이크, 옆에 새우와 채소. 선택을 앞둔 정적인 구도.

head: Steak Americans knew.
A show they didn’t.
body: Aoki picked the first path. Chefs cooked steak, chicken and shrimp on a steel grill right in front of guests, with flashing knives and flying food.
The menu was familiar. The experience was something new.

image.label: A chef flipping shrimp toward a laughing table
image.brief: 셰프가 새우를 공중으로 던지고 손님들이 웃는 장면. 인물은 일반적인 모습, 실존 인물 얼굴 없음. 1970년대 의상.

head: Slow at first.
Then a line out the door.
body: A story often told: the restaurant struggled for months, until a well-known food critic praised it.
After that, New Yorkers came for the show, and Benihana began opening in other cities.

image.label: A queue of diners outside a restaurant at night
image.brief: 밤거리 식당 앞에 늘어선 손님 줄. 1960~70년대 뉴욕 분위기. 간판 로고 없음.

slides.label: seats around each grill, filled with groups of strangers
body: Guests waited at the bar until eight were ready, then sat down together. One chef cooked for the whole table at once, so every seat was used and every meal started on time.

image.label: Eight diners seated around one grill
image.brief: 철판 하나를 ㄷ자로 둘러싼 8개의 좌석, 서로 모르는 손님들이 함께 앉은 장면. 위에서 내려다본 구도.

head: The show was also
the business model.
body: With cooking at the table, the back kitchen could be small, leaving more room for paying seats. A short menu meant little wasted food and simple prep.
Because the show set the pace, meals ended sooner than a typical dinner, and tables turned faster.

image.label: A tiny prep kitchen beside a busy dining room
image.brief: 작은 준비 주방 옆으로 붐비는 넓은 식당 홀이 보이는 단면도 스타일 일러스트.

head: From one small room
to a national chain.
body: Over the next two decades, Benihana spread across the United States. Its operations became a well-known Harvard Business School case.
The flames and jokes looked like fun. Underneath, every part was doing a job.

image.label: A map of the United States with glowing dots
image.brief: 미국 지도 위에 도시마다 불빛 점이 켜지는 그래픽. 빈티지 1980년대 색감.

head: Every piece paid twice:
for guests and the books.
body: The table grill was entertainment and a smaller kitchen. The short menu was easy for diners and cut waste. Seating groups of eight filled every chair.
Strong businesses work when their activities fit together and support each other.

image.label: Interlocking gears made of grill, knife and chairs
image.brief: 철판, 칼, 의자가 톱니바퀴처럼 맞물려 돌아가는 그래픽.

head: Make the experience
do the hard work.
body: The best customer experience can also cut costs and raise capacity, if you design both together.
**Try it today:** pick one thing customers love about you. Could it also save you time, space or waste?

image.label: An empty grill table glowing after service
image.brief: 영업이 끝난 뒤 은은히 빛나는 빈 철판 테이블. 고요한 마무리 톤.

factChecks.note: 1964년 뉴욕 맨해튼(웨스트 56번가)에 첫 Benihana 개점, 테이블 4개 규모는 Benihana 공식 연혁과 여러 언론 보도 기준입니다. 테이블 수는 자료마다 표현이 조금 달라 원문 확인이 필요합니다. → [2026-11-02 확인] 1964년 웨스트 56번가, 테이블 4개 확인.
Rocky(Hiroaki) Aoki가 아이스크림 트럭 등으로 창업 자금을 모았다는 이야기는 널리 전해지지만 금액은 자료마다 달라 카드에서는 "reportedly"로만 적고 금액은 넣지 않았습니다.
그릴 테이블당 8석, 바에서 손님을 8명 단위로 모아 앉히는 방식, 작은 주방과 제한된 메뉴(스테이크·닭고기·새우)는 Harvard Business School 케이스 "Benihana of Tokyo"(1972) 기준입니다.

개업 초기 손님이 적다가 유명 음식 평론가(New York Herald Tribune의 Clementine Paddleford로 알려짐)의 호평 후 붐볐다는 이야기는 전해지는 일화라 "a story often told"로 표시하고 평론가 이름은 넣지 않았습니다. → [2026-11-02 확인] 평론가 호평 일화는 이번 검색에서 미확인. 초기 부진 기간은 자료마다 다름.
식사 시간이 일반 저녁 식사보다 짧았다는 점은 HBS 케이스 내용입니다. 구체적인 분 단위 수치는 넣지 않았습니다.
1980년대까지 미국 전역으로 확장했다는 점은 정성적으로만 적었습니다. 연도별 매장 수는 회사 연혁으로 확인 후 필요 시 추가하세요.

sources.text: Sasser, W. E. & Klug, J. (1972). Benihana of Tokyo. Harvard Business School case
The New York Times, obituary of Rocky Aoki (2008)
